paragraphs.source_en: The maid set a chintz cushion before the alcove, said to the guest, “Please sit here,” and withdrew. Left alone, Suzuki looked around the room: in the alcove hung a fake calligraphic painting by Mokuan reading “Flowers Bloom, Spring Comes to All Nations,” and there was also a cheap Kyoto celadon vase with several sprigs of winter cherry in it. After inspecting these things, he happened to glance at the cushion the maid had set out for him, and there, before he knew it, sat a cat with perfect composure. Needless to say, that celebrated personage was none other than myself. At that moment, a small disturbance rose in Suzuki’s breast. The cushion had plainly been placed especially for him, yet before he could sit on it, some odd animal was squatting there with lordly unconcern. This was the first condition that upset Suzuki’s mental equilibrium. If the cushion, after being offered to Suzuki, had remained empty and open to the spring breeze, then perhaps, out of deliberate modesty, Suzuki would have endured sitting on the hard tatami until the master said, “Please, do sit on it.” But the one who had climbed unbidden onto the cushion he was bound sooner or later to occupy was, if it had been a person, someone he might have yielded to; that it was a cat was simply outrageous. That made him feel doubly displeased. This was the second condition that upset Suzuki’s mental equilibrium. Finally, the cat’s attitude was what irritated him most of all. Did it show the slightest sign of feeling sorry? Not at all. Instead, it sat arrogantly on a cushion to which it had no right whatever, blinking its round, unamiable eyes and staring into Suzuki’s face as if to say, “And who might you be?” This was the third condition that destroyed Suzuki’s equilibrium. With so much to complain of, Suzuki might well have seized me by the scruff of the neck and dragged me off the cushion, yet he merely looked at me in silence. Surely a dignified human being could not have been afraid of a cat like me; so why did he not quickly dispose of me and vent his displeasure? It seems this was entirely due to Suzuki’s cautious desire to preserve his dignity as a human being. If force were the question, even a child of three feet could toss me up and down at will; but from the standpoint of dignity, even Suzuki Tojuro, that trusty right arm of Mr. Kaneda, could do nothing against this Great Cat Bodhisattva enthroned at the center of a two-foot-square seat. Even if no one else was present, to quarrel with a cat over a seat would still touch, however slightly, upon human dignity. To make a serious issue of right and wrong with a cat as one’s opponent hardly seems the conduct of a grown man; it is rather ridiculous. To avoid such a dishonorable affair, he had no choice but to endure the awkward situation. Yet precisely because he had to endure it, his hatred of the cat grew all the stronger. From time to time Suzuki looked at me, and each time his face grew sour and miserable. I found it highly amusing to look up at Suzuki’s aggrieved expression, so I suppressed my laughter as best I could and put on an air of complete innocence.

paragraphs.source_zh: 女仆把印花布的坐垫摆放在“壁龛”前，对客人说了声“您请坐”，就退下来了。剩下铃木君一个人，他环视了一下室内：壁龛里挂着一幅木庵的“花开万国春”的赝品字画，还有一个京都烧制的廉价青瓷花瓶，瓶中插着几枝“寒樱”。他看过这些后，无心地往女仆给他摆好的坐垫看了一眼，不知什么时候，一只猫大模大样地坐在上面。不说也明白，它就是鼎鼎大名的在下喽。这时，铃木君的内心里一瞬间涌起了一阵波澜，这个坐垫不用说是特地为他放的，而在他坐上去之前，就被一只奇怪的动物大模大样地蹲在上面，这是破坏他心理平衡的第一个条件。如果这个坐垫在请铃木君坐上去之前，空荡荡任凭春风吹拂，那么也许铃木君为了表示谦恭之意，会在主人说声“请坐上去”之前，就在硬邦邦的铺席上一直忍耐下去。但是，在迟早应由自己占有的坐垫上，不打招呼就坐上去的如果是人，那还可以忍让，可居然是只猫儿，真是岂有此理。这更使他感到加倍的不愉快。这是破坏铃木君心理平衡的第二个条件。最后，还有这只猫儿的态度更惹他生气。它哪里有半点儿感到内疚的神色呀！而且居然以傲岸不逊的态度，坐在根本无权坐的坐垫上，眨着那双不惹人喜爱的圆眼睛，注视着铃木君的脸，仿佛在说“你老兄是谁呀？”这是破坏铃木君心理平衡的第三个条件。既然铃木君如此的不满，他本来满可以抓起我的脖子把我从坐垫上一把揪下来，可是铃木君却一声不响地瞧着我。按理说一个堂堂的人，不应该怕我这只猫儿而不动手，那么他为什么不早早处置我来发泄他的不满呢？看来这完全是出自铃木君为了维持自己作为人的体面而自重的心理。假如诉之暴力，那么三尺童子也可以上下翻弄我，但从体面这点来看，即便这位金田君的肱股之臣铃木藤十郎，也拿我这个盘踞在这二尺见方宝座上的猫大菩萨毫无办法。尽管旁边无人，但和猫争座位总多少要关系到人的尊严。认真地以猫儿为对手争个是非曲直，总显得不像是个男子汉所为，未免滑稽可笑。为了避免这种有损名誉的事，就只好忍受这种尴尬局面。然而，正因为他必须忍受这种局面，所以他对猫儿的憎恨也就更加强烈。铃木君不时地瞧我一眼，每次都显出一副哭丧脸儿。我仰望着铃木君那副表情感到非常有趣，于是我尽量忍住笑意，作出一副若无其事的样子。

paragraphs.source_en: While this pantomime was being performed between Suzuki and me, the master, having straightened his clothes, came back from the privy, said “Ah,” and sat down. Since not even a trace remained of the calling card he had been holding, it appeared that the name of Suzuki Tojuro had been sentenced to life imprisonment in that foul-smelling place. I was just thinking to myself, “That calling card has met with a terrible misfortune!” At that very moment, the master seized me by the scruff of the neck and said, “You rascal!” Then he flung me out onto the veranda.
